LIMBA.CONTENTS:
OVERVIEW
I have a HO railroad set up that I put together 25-30 years ago. Its somewhat complex, sitting on a 12 foot by 4 foot table, and can run two trains independently on the mainline and have one or two more operating in a rail yard complete with sidings and a turntable. There are 13 rail switches (Y's) (with 11 controls since there are two pairs that are wired to operate together). There is a crossover and a reversing track on the main line. And there are 14 track blocks, sections of track that have independent power controls.
Needless to say, this is rather complex to operate, especially for one person. In addition to the 11 buttons to control the 13 switches, there are 14 power controls for the different blocks, 3 rheostats to control speed, 4 forward-off-reverse controls, and a control for the turntable. These are spread over two control panels.
One has to prevent trains from both derailing and crashing. Derailing occurs most commonly when a train tries to pass over a switch that is set incorrectly. It can also occur when a train is moving too fast around a curve or over a bridge. Collisions can occur when two trains converge on a switch or if two trains are on the same track and one is going faster than the other. The standard approach to preventing collisions is to ensure that only one train at a time is in a track block.
I want to control this setup from my computer. Moreover, I want to have a high level control so I can say things like "Take train A out of the yard, go around the outer loop 3 times, then around the inner loop twice, then reverse directions and go around the outer loop twice more before bringing the train back into the yard." At the same time, I want to ensure that the trains do not crash or derail. This is the system that should be written. Moreover it should be written as a generic system, able to control other layouts.
UNDERLYING HARDWARE
In order to have computer control of the HO layout, one needs to enable the computer to both understand the current conditions, for example, what state switches are in and where trains are, and to control things.
Our layout, because it is relatively old, used all manual controls. These include rheostats, buttons for each switch, and controls to select the power source and direction for each track block. Shortly after the layout was built, trains started to supportDigital Command Control (DCC). Here there is continuous power to all rails and the control is in the engine. DCC sends signals to the engines via pulses on top of the rail power. This is done using special controllers that are attached to the circuit. This allows each engine to independently go forwards or backwards and to controls speed. This type of control is much simpler and closer to the real world.
DCC, however, is starting to fall out of favor. Today one can find the equivalent controls using WiFi so that the engines can be controlled from ones phone or tablet and no special hardware is required. While DCC has been standardized, WiFi control has not.
While it is possible to create a circuit that would effectively actuate the original set of controls for the HO layout, we decided that it made more sense to upgrade the engines to use the latest technology. Again, while we could do this via DCC (there are Arduino-based DCC controllers), we decided that we wanted to go with WiFi and use the LocoFi implementation for the engines. Thus we have provided full power to all track segments and have the engines control their own speed and direction using embedded LocoFi controllers.
This means that the system needs to control the switches and signals, detect of the state of the trains, and control the speed and direction of the various engines. It does not need to control the power to the blocks. We inserted photo diodes in the tracks at key locations. These include on each side the gap between track blocks to detect when a train moves from one block to another; on entry to the two inputs to a switch to ensure the switch is set correctly before the train goes over it; and at locations where we might want a train to stop (red signal) before entering a new block. The sensors we use are not perfect and can given occasional false positive and false negative outputs. The program needs to accommodate this.
To detect train positions and control switches and signals we designed and built a set of track controllers. Each of these can control 3 switches, handle 8 sensors (photo-diodes), and set 6 signals. An additional controller can handle up to 40 sensors. These compliment the LocoFi engine controllers which control engine speed and direction. All controllers communicate over local WiFi using mDNS and short (4-64 byte) UDP messages. For the purpose of the software, one can assume the hardware is stable and not part of the program.
SOFTWARE OVERVIEW
The software we envision would allow both manual and automatic control of the complete layout. The user interface would display the current state of the switches, signals, and trains as the system knows them. It would let the user control the switches and signals directly. It would provide control of the engines using an interface similar to that offered by the LocoFi phone app, emulating the messages it sends to the engines.
The standard way of displaying a train layout, both in model railroading and for real trains, is to have an display an abstraction of the actual layout. This has a homomorphic mapping with the actual layout, which may omit some details such as curves. For a complex layout, there can be multiple such abstract displays that have connections from one to another. This can be seen in our initial system where the two control panels each have their own abstraction. The software we envision should provide such an abstraction as part of the interface and allow the user to control the various layout components from this abstraction. Note that since the system works in terms of this abstract layout, it cannot be dependent on absolute train positions.
The abstract layout is described in an XML file that provides positions for the tracks, switches, signals, sensors, and block boundaries. Tracks are indicated by connections between points (which may or may not relate to switches, signals or sensors). These are given in an arbitrary coordinate system and may not be exact. The software should load this file, make almost-straight lines straight, ensure that the track layout makes sense, associate points with blocks, and generally ensure the consistency of the input and the layout.
Both our hardware and the LocoFi hardware use mDNS over local WiFi to find the controlling application (or vice versa). Both use short UDP messages containing commands (to the hardware, e.g., engine speed, set switch, set signal) and status reports (e.g., sensor changed). The control software should find and connect to these devices, send them commands appropriately, and use them to monitor the state of the engines and layout. Moreover, the software should attempt to correct sensor errors whenever possible.
The software should to ensure the stability and safety of the system. It should prevent two trains from being in the same block at the same time. Because the system does not have absolute train position information, this is sufficient to prevent collisions. The system should ensure that a switch is set property before a train can pass over it. It should ensure that signals are set correctly and that trains obeyed the signals. It should enforce speed limits on specific sections of track (between two specified sensors).
The software should also provide the type of high level control that we envision where one could define a route for a train and have the train correctly follow that route while obeying the various safety conditions. It should identify loops from the layout as well as possible starting and ending points for a route.
The system should also be flexible and extensible. The embedded sensors do not provide complete information about train position. They have problems understanding the initial conditions, can miss trains at times, and there are significant spans of track with no sensors. The system should optionally allow a video camera aimed at the track to be used to obtain better information about the current state of trains. Note this isn't perfect either since there might be portions of the track, for example, tunnels, that would not be visible to the camera. The system should also be flexible in that it should be able to handle layouts beyond ours. We do not include examples of all types of tracks and conditions. For example, initially we only have 2-way switches while 3-way switches exist, and we have no X-crossings which induce other types of anti-collision constraints.
The system is being designed for personal, local use. As such no access control is needed and data protection, backup, and system integreity are not particularly important.

# HO Railroad Control System - Requirements Specification
## 1. SYSTEM OVERVIEW AND SCOPE
### 1.1 System Purpose The HO Railroad Control System provides computer-based control of a complex model railroad layout with the capability for both manual and automatic train operation while ensuring safety through collision and derailment prevention.
### 1.2 System Scope - Control of switches, signals, and trains on complex layout (13 switches, 14 track blocks) - Manual and high-level automatic train control interfaces - Safety enforcement mechanisms to prevent collisions and derailments - Support for multiple layout abstraction layers - Generic architecture supporting various railroad layouts - Integration with existing hardware including WiFi-enabled controllers
## 2. SYSTEM COMPONENTS
### 2.1 Layout Abstraction Engine - XML-based layout definition parser - Coordinate system normalization and track validation - Block boundary identification and association - Abstract display generation for user interface - Route identification and loop detection algorithms
### 2.2 Hardware Communication Layer - mDNS discovery of track controllers over local WiFi - UDP message handling for commands and status reports - Device connection management and monitoring - Command queuing and error handling - Sensor data processing with noise filtering
### 2.3 Train Control Module - Engine speed and direction control (emulating LocoFi protocol) - Route planning and execution engine - Automatic train scheduling and pathfinding - Speed limit enforcement between sensors - Engine state monitoring and reporting
### 2.4 Safety Management System - Block occupancy detection and management - Switch position validation before train passage - Signal enforcement and train compliance monitoring - Collision prevention algorithms (single train per block) - Derailment prevention mechanisms - Emergency stop capabilities
### 2.5 User Interface Layer - Real-time layout visualization with current state display - Manual control of switches, signals, and trains - High-level route definition interface - Sensor status monitoring - Video camera integration for enhanced position tracking
### 2.6 Data Management System - Layout configuration storage and retrieval (XML format) - Train movement history logging - System state persistence - Configuration backup and restore capabilities
## 3. REQUIREMENTS SPECIFICATIONS
### 3.1 Functional Requirements
#### 3.1.1 Layout Abstraction - **R-3.1.1**: Parse XML layout definition files containing track points, switches, signals, sensors, and block boundaries - **R-3.1.2**: Validate track topology for consistency and logical connections - **R-3.1.3**: Normalize coordinate system to ensure straight lines appear straight in display - **R-3.1.4**: Automatically associate points with track blocks based on sensor locations - **R-3.1.5**: Identify and mark loop structures within the layout for route planning - **R-3.1.6**: Determine valid starting and ending points for train routes
#### 3.1.2 Hardware Integration - **R-3.1.7**: Discover track controllers using mDNS over local WiFi network - **R-3.1.8**: Establish stable UDP communication channels with all controllers - **R-3.1.9**: Send control commands (switch set, signal set, engine speed/direction) to appropriate controllers - **R-3.1.10**: Receive and process sensor status reports from controllers - **R-3.1.11**: Handle intermittent communication failures with graceful degradation - **R-3.1.12**: Implement message acknowledgment and retransmission for critical commands
#### 3.1.3 Train Control - **R-3.1.13**: Provide engine control interface similar to LocoFi mobile app - **R-3.1.14**: Support speed and direction control for individual engines - **R-3.1.15**: Implement automatic route execution with pathfinding algorithms - **R-3.1.16**: Enforce speed limits between specified sensor points - **R-3.1.17**: Track train positions within the abstract layout space - **R-3.1.18**: Support multiple trains operating simultaneously on different routes
#### 3.1.4 Safety Management - **R-3.1.19**: Prevent multiple trains from occupying the same track block simultaneously - **R-3.1.20**: Validate switch positions before allowing train passage through switches - **R-3.1.21**: Monitor signal states and ensure trains respect signal indications - **R-3.1.22**: Implement speed limit enforcement for specific track sections - **R-3.1.23**: Detect and prevent potential collision scenarios - **R-3.1.24**: Handle sensor false positives and negatives with error correction mechanisms
#### 3.1.5 User Interface - **R-3.1.25**: Display real-time layout state with visual representation of switches, signals, and trains - **R-3.1.26**: Provide manual control interface for switches, signals, and engines - **R-3.1.27**: Enable high-level route definition through intuitive graphical interface - **R-3.1.28**: Show sensor status and error conditions to user - **R-3.1.29**: Integrate video camera feed for enhanced train position tracking when available
### 3.2 Non-Functional Requirements
#### 3.2.1 Performance - **R-3.2.1**: Real-time response time for sensor data processing (<50ms) - **R-3.2.2**: Command execution latency for control operations (<100ms) - **R-3.2.3**: Support for real-time display updates (30+ FPS) - **R-3.2.4**: Efficient route planning algorithms for complex layouts
#### 3.2.2 Reliability - **R-3.2.5**: System stability with no user intervention required for normal operation - **R-3.2.6**: Graceful degradation when hardware components fail - **R-3.2.7**: Automatic recovery from communication failures - **R-3.2.8**: Data integrity maintenance during system operation
#### 3.2.3 Safety and Security - **R-3.2.9**: Complete prevention of train collisions through block occupancy management - **R-3.2.10**: Prevention of derailments through proper switch positioning enforcement - **R-3.2.11**: Emergency stop capability for immediate system halt - **R-3.2.12**: No external access control required (local use only)
#### 3.2.4 Extensibility - **R-3.2.13**: Generic architecture supporting different types of track layouts - **R-3.2.14**: Support for additional switch types (3-way, X-crossings) - **R-3.2.15**: Modular design allowing addition of new hardware controllers - **R-3.2.16**: Configurable sensor types and integration capabilities
#### 3.2.5 Usability - **R-3.2.17**: Intuitive graphical user interface for manual control operations - **R-3.2.18**: Clear visual feedback for all system states and operations - **R-3.2.19**: Easy route definition and modification capabilities - **R-3.2.20**: Comprehensive error reporting and troubleshooting information
### 3.3 Data Requirements
#### 3.3.1 Layout Data - **R-3.3.1**: XML configuration files describing track topology - **R-3.3.2**: Coordinate point definitions for all layout elements - **R-3.3.3**: Switch configuration and control mappings - **R-3.3.4**: Sensor placement and identification data - **R-3.3.5**: Block boundary definitions and associated track segments
#### 3.3.2 System State Data - **R-3.3.6**: Current switch positions (active/inactive) - **R-3.3.7**: Signal states (red/yellow/green/unknown) - **R-3.3.8**: Train positions within abstract layout space - **R-3.3.9**: Block occupancy status (occupied/free) - **R-3.3.10**: Engine speed and direction settings
### 3.4 Interface Requirements
#### 3.4.1 User Interface - **R-3.4.1**: Graphical display of abstract layout with current state visualization - **R-3.4.2**: Interactive controls for switches, signals, and train operations - **R-3.4.3**: Route definition and execution interface - **R-3.4.4**: Sensor status monitoring panel - **R-3.4.5**: Video feed integration with position tracking overlay
#### 3.4.2 Hardware Interface - **R-3.4.6**: mDNS discovery protocol implementation for device detection - **R-3.4.7**: UDP communication layer for command and status transmission - **R-3.4.8**: Command message format specification for controller compatibility - **R-3.4.9**: Status report format for sensor and device state information
## 4. SYSTEM CONSTRAINTS
### 4.1 Hardware Constraints - **C-4.1**: Existing layout uses WiFi-enabled controllers with UDP communication protocol - **C-4.2**: Switches are limited to 13 physical switches with specific control requirements - **C-4.3**: Track blocks defined by sensor placement and connection topology - **C-4.4**: Video camera integration is optional but supported
### 4.2 Operational Constraints - **C-4.5**: System designed for local network operation only (no external access) - **C-4.6**: Real-time safety enforcement required for collision prevention - **C-4.7**: No data backup or integrity protection requirements - **C-4.8**: No concurrent user access restrictions
### 4.3 Development Constraints - **C-4.9**: Must support existing LocoFi protocol for engine control - **C-4.10**: XML-based configuration format required for layout definition - **C-4.11**: No external dependencies or third-party software requirements - **C-4.12**: Local system performance optimization required
## 5. ASSUMPTIONS AND DEPENDENCIES
### 5.1 Assumptions - **A-5.1**: All hardware controllers will support standard UDP communication protocol - **A-5.2**: Network connectivity will be stable for local operation - **A-5.3**: Users will have basic understanding of railroad operations and terminology - **A-5.4**: Layout topology will remain relatively static during system operation
### 5.2 Dependencies - **D-5.1**: Successful hardware discovery requires active network connectivity - **D-5.2**: Sensor data accuracy depends on proper physical sensor placement - **D-5.3**: Route planning algorithms depend on accurate layout topology data - **D-5.4**: Video integration requires compatible camera hardware and drivers
